title: EAMT 2026 Highlights Paper Does Not Vary Iteration
layman_summary: A 2026 translation-editing paper varies how broad AI error highlights are but never tests repeating or double-checking a fix, so it does not overlap with this project's core comparison.
summary: This artifact closes the single remaining unverified lead flagged by the prior literature-search artifact (art_QAQK2EUnuaCO): the EAMT 2026 paper 'Smarter edits? Post-editing with error highlights and translation suggestions' (van Tellingen et al., ACL Anthology 2026.eamt-1.41, arXiv:2605.21135v2). The paper was located via two verbatim searches (both returning it as a top hit), fetched in full (arXiv HTML v2, 67.5k chars), and classified against art_QAQK2EUnuaCO's exact four-way decision rule (separates the factors / bundles the factors / varies only one factor / out of scope) using fetch_grep for quoted primary-text evidence. The paper studies four post-editing conditions for professional En-Nl translators: (1) regular PE with no assistance; (2) PE + QE-derived highlights (H-QE) from xCOMET-XXL spans; (3) PE + APE-derived highlights (H-APE), spans obtained by Levenshtein-diffing the raw MT output against a single xTower-Instruct-13B-v0.1 auto-post-edited version; (4) PE + APE correction suggestions (S-APE), the H-APE spans plus the xTower replacement text shown to the translator. Quoted methods text confirms xTower is invoked exactly once per sentence -- one xCOMET-XXL scoring pass feeds one xTower correction pass, reused by both H-APE and S-APE -- with no re-scoring or repeated correction call anywhere in the pipeline. A full-text regex sweep for iteration language (iterat|re-check|re-verif|re-flag|second pass|repeat, case-insensitive) returns exactly 2 matches, both referring to 'repeated measures ANOVA' (a statistical test design), not to repeated correction attempts -- zero genuine iteration/re-verification language exists in the paper, mirroring art_QAQK2EUnuaCO's finding for Sharma (2025). Localization breadth DOES vary across conditions: H-QE's xCOMET spans are narrower (sometimes single characters) while H-APE/S-APE's diff-derived spans are broader and score higher against human oracle edits (Appendix A). VERDICT: the paper 'varies only one factor' -- localization breadth via differing span-source models -- with no iteration/re-verification axis present in any of its four conditions; iteration is absent from the whole design, not held fixed as a controlled second variable. A second, independent difference from this project's protocol is also documented: the EAMT paper is a human-translator productivity/UX study (keystrokes, post-editing time, DA quality ratings, satisfaction surveys, interviews) rather than an automated repair-loop study measuring fix rate, regression rate, or delta-COMET on LLM-generated repairs -- it is not attempting the same measurement this project's C1-vs-C2 protocol makes, independent of the localization/iteration finding. A Step-6 sweep (two additional queries) found no closer or distinct EAMT 2026 candidate; the only 'iterative' MT-refinement hit returned was a 2024 (not 2026) TEaR-family paper already covered by the prior artifact. This closes the project's final open literature-search item: across all seven candidates now checked (the prior artifact's six plus this one), none independently varies both localization breadth and iteration/re-verification as two separately measured factors while holding the other fixed -- the project's novelty claim, scoped to MT automatic post-editing / scoped span editing, requires NO further narrowing.
answer:
The EAMT 2026 candidate flagged as the prior artifact's (art_QAQK2EUnuaCO) sole open item -- 'Smarter edits? Post-editing with error highlights and translation suggestions' (van Tellingen et al., ACL Anthology 2026.eamt-1.41, arXiv:2605.21135v2) [1][2][3] -- was located via two verbatim searches that both return it as a top hit [4][5], fetched in full [1], and classified with quoted primary-text evidence [1].

The paper's four post-editing conditions are: (1) regular PE, no assistance; (2) H-QE, error highlights from xCOMET-XXL span detection; (3) H-APE, error highlights obtained by Levenshtein-diffing the raw MT output against a single xTower-Instruct-13B-v0.1 auto-post-edited version; (4) S-APE, the H-APE spans paired with the xTower correction text itself shown to the translator [1]. Quoted methods text: 'Error spans: xCOMET-XXL was used to automatically identify error spans (H-QE)... The texts and error spans obtained from xCOMET were put into xTower-Instruct-13B-v0.1 to generate error explanations and translation corrections (APE)... We compared the raw MT output and APE'd sentence using Levenshtein distance. The spans that differ between MT and APE were highlighted as errors' [1]. This confirms xTower is invoked exactly once per sentence -- a single generation pass, with H-APE and S-APE both derived post-hoc from that one output -- not an iterated or checker-guided loop.

A full-text regex sweep of the entire paper for iteration/re-verification language (iterat|re-check|re-verif|re-flag|second pass|repeat, case-insensitive) returns exactly 2 matches, both 'repeated measures ANOVA' -- a statistical test design, not repeated correction attempts [1]. Zero genuine iteration language exists anywhere in the paper, directly mirroring art_QAQK2EUnuaCO's finding that Sharma (2025) contained zero occurrences of 'iterat' [6].

Localization breadth DOES vary across conditions, confirmed by quoted text: H-QE spans 'sometimes only cover parts of words' and include 'highlights that were not easily interpretable, e.g. single characters,' while H-APE/S-APE's diff-derived spans are broader and score higher against human oracle edits in the paper's own AP/AUC overlap analysis (Appendix A) [1].

Applying art_QAQK2EUnuaCO's exact four-way decision rule (separates the factors / bundles the factors / varies only one factor / out of scope) [6], the verdict is 'varies only one factor': the paper varies localization breadth (narrow xCOMET spans vs. broader diff-derived spans) but never varies iteration/re-verification of a repair -- iteration is absent from every one of the four conditions, not held fixed as a controlled second variable [1]. This is NOT the same as this project's C1-vs-C2 design, which requires BOTH breadth and iteration to be independently varied while holding the other fixed.

A second, independent axis of difference from this project's protocol is also documented: the EAMT paper is a human-translator productivity and user-experience study -- its outcome measures are keystrokes, post-editing time, direct-assessment quality ratings, perceived-usefulness surveys, and semi-structured interviews (Sections 4.1-4.7) [1] -- not an automated repair-loop study measuring fix rate, regression rate, or delta-COMET on LLM-generated repairs applied without a human editor. This means the paper is not even attempting the same measurement this project's protocol makes, independent of and in addition to the localization/iteration finding.

A Step-6 sweep of two additional queries ('EAMT 2026 iterative repair verification translation' and 'EAMT 2026 CEGIS translation post-editing') found no closer or distinct EAMT 2026 candidate that might separate the two factors [7][8]. The only genuinely 'iterative' MT-refinement paper surfaced was 'Iterative Translation Refinement with Large Language Models' (Chen et al.) -- but this is EAMT **2024**, not 2026, and is a TEaR-family self-refinement paper already checked and classified by the prior artifact (art_QAQK2EUnuaCO found TEaR varies iteration count while holding localization/estimation scope fixed -- a one-dimensional finding, not a factor-separating design) [6][7].

CONCLUSION: This closes the project's final open literature-search item. Across all seven candidates now checked (the prior artifact's six -- TEaR, two WMT25 QE-informed correction systems, xTower's own paper, SSPO, TranslationCorrect, and a non-MT self-localization paper -- plus this EAMT 2026 candidate), none independently varies both localization breadth and iteration/re-verification of a repair as two separately measured factors while holding the other fixed. The project's novelty claim, scoped specifically to MT automatic post-editing / scoped span editing (per art_QAQK2EUnuaCO's recommended wording, rather than self-correction research broadly) [6], requires NO further narrowing based on this candidate. Confidence is high: the classification rests on quoted primary-text evidence from a full fetch of the paper (not abstract-only reading), a complete regex sweep of the entire document text for iteration language (2/2 matches independently confirmed as statistical, not methodological), and a targeted secondary search that found no alternative candidate.

follow_up_questions: The paper's own SmartPE interface and data/code are open-sourced (github.com/fatalinha/smarter-edits, github.com/fatalinha/SmartPE) -- would this project's automated repair-loop protocol benefit from adapting SmartPE's human-annotation interface for a human-evaluation arm, even though the current project measures automated fix rate rather than human productivity?

art_QAQK2EUnuaCO flagged that ACL-Anthology-native search would likely surface more candidates than the free OpenAlex/Crossref scholarly backend used across both artifacts -- should a follow-up literature pass specifically query ACL Anthology's own search interface for MT repair-localization papers before the project's Related Work section is finalized, given that this artifact's own EAMT 2026 lead was found only via general web search, not scholarly-mode search?

Should the project's Related Work section explicitly cite this artifact and art_QAQK2EUnuaCO together as a paired closing statement (six-candidate sweep plus this seventh, final candidate), presenting the novelty claim as resting on seven independently verified negatives rather than presenting them as two separate literature-search efforts?
